title: Prehabilitation to improve outcomes following transcatheter aortic valve implantation
official: A randomised controlled trial of multI-moDal prEhAbiLitation in patients with severe aortic stenosis awaiting Transcatheter Aortic Valve Implantation: The IDEAL-TAVI Study
summary:
Background and study aims
Aortic stenosis is a condition in which the aortic valve, one of the heart's four valves, becomes narrowed. This restricts blood flow out of the heart and can cause symptoms such as breathlessness, chest pain and fainting. If left untreated, severe aortic stenosis can be life-threatening. Transcatheter aortic valve implantation (TAVI) is a minimally invasive procedure in which a new heart valve is inserted within the narrowed valve, usually through a blood vessel in the leg. This avoids the need for open-heart surgery.

Although TAVI is very effective, some patients do not experience the expected improvement in their symptoms or quality of life. This is particularly true for people living with frailty, who may also be more likely to experience complications and have a slower recovery. There is some evidence that frailty may be improved through interventions such as exercise and nutritional support. Prehabilitation is like training for the procedure; it combines gentle exercise, nutritional support, and advice to support your well-being. This preparation is intended to help patients feel stronger and more confident before their procedure, which may lead to better recovery and outcomes afterwards. Although prehabilitation has shown benefits in patients undergoing surgery, it is not yet known whether it is suitable or beneficial for patients awaiting TAVI.

The IDEAL-TAVI Pilot Study aims to investigate whether an eight-week prehabilitation programme can be safely and practically delivered to patients with frailty awaiting TAVI, and whether it is acceptable to patients. The findings will help inform the design of a larger study to determine whether prehabilitation improves recovery and outcomes following TAVI.

Who can participate?
Adults aged 18 years or older with severe symptomatic aortic stenosis who are living with frailty and are awaiting a planned TAVI procedure may be eligible to participate.

What does the study involve?
The study aims to recruit 60 participants, who will be randomly allocated to one of two groups. Approximately two-thirds will receive an eight-week prehabilitation programme in addition to their usual care, while the remaining third will continue to receive usual care alone.

The prehabilitation programme includes three components:
- Exercise: An initial face-to-face assessment with a physiotherapist to develop an individualised exercise programme, followed by weekly supervised virtual exercise sessions and additional home-based exercises.
- Nutritional support: Assessment and advice from a dietitian to optimise nutritional intake, including dietary recommendations and nutritional supplements where required.
- Educational support: Information and resources to help patients understand their condition, prepare for their procedure and manage their recovery.

All participants will undergo assessments at the beginning of the study, immediately before their TAVI procedure and approximately 6 months afterwards. These will include questionnaires about their health and quality of life, walking and balance tests, measurements of muscle strength and body composition, and activity monitoring using a wearable fitness tracker. Some participants receiving prehabilitation may also be invited to take part in an optional interview to share their experiences of the programme.

What are the possible benefits and risks of participating?
Participants receiving prehabilitation may experience improvements in their physical fitness, strength and confidence before TAVI, which could support their recovery afterwards. However, these benefits cannot be guaranteed. All participants will contribute valuable information that may help improve care for future patients undergoing TAVI.

The exercise programme is designed to be gentle and tailored to each participant's abilities. However, physical activity may cause muscle soreness, fatigue or, rarely, minor injury. Due to their underlying heart condition, some participants may experience symptoms such as breathlessness, chest discomfort or dizziness during exercise. A physiotherapist will assess participants before starting the programme to minimise these risks.

Where is the study run from?
Guy's and St. Thomas' NHS Foundation Trust 

When is the study starting and how long is it expected to run for?
December 2026 to June 2028 

Who is funding the study?
Edwards Lifesciences (UK)

Who is the main contact?
Dr Rea Ganatra, rea.ganatra@nhs.net

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
1. Aged ≥18 years
2. Symptomatic severe AS and accepted for TAVI by the treating TAVI multidisciplinary team (i.e. echocardiographic findings consistent with severe AS, including an aortic valve area ≤1.0 cm², indexed aortic valve area ≤0.6 cm²/m², mean transvalvular gradient ≥40 mmHg and/or peak aortic jet velocity ≥4.0 m/s, or with integrated clinical assessment used where discordant parameters are seen)
3. Clinical Frailty Scale score 3-5
4. Able and willing to provide informed consent and participate in study procedures
Exclusion criteria:
1. Critical AS, defined as AVA ≤0.6 cm², mean transvalvular gradient ≥60 mmHg or peak aortic jet velocity ≥5.0 m/s;
2. Previous cardiac syncope considered attributable to AS
3. Unstable angina (CCS class III–IV)
4. Severe left ventricular systolic impairment (LVEF <35%)
5. Greater than Stage 2 extra-aortic cardiac damage, according to the prespecified cardiac damage staging system
6. Significant non-cardiac limitation that, in the opinion of the investigator or treating clinical team, would prevent safe participation in the exercise intervention
7. Severe obstructive pulmonary disease
8. Scheduled TAVI date <8 weeks from enrolment
9. Concurrent participation in another research study where participation would require deviation from the IDEAL-TAVI protocol or otherwise interfere with the intervention or study outcomes
